title: Session 2: Time
text:
A packet arrives from Mars
The MAVEN header says the data were taken at

SCLK 3/0812345678.32768

When was that, in UTC? And where was MAVEN?

To answer, SPICE needs two pieces of knowledge that live in kernels:

how Earth’s civil time relates to uniform physical time → LSK
how this spacecraft’s clock relates to physical time → SCLK

Today: where those two files come from, and why they look the way they do.

Open with the concrete question. Everyone in data systems has seen a raw clock value in a packet header; few have thought about what it takes to turn it into a UTC string. The rest of the talk builds up the two kernels that answer it.

title: Session 2: Time
text:
Two ways to count time


Solar time (UT1)

Noon = Sun over the prime meridian
Follows Earth’s rotation, which is irregular and slowing (~ms per day)
What humans live by


Atomic time (TAI)

Weighted average of hundreds of atomic clocks worldwide
Every second is an SI second (cesium-133)
Perfectly uniform, ignores the Sun





UTC ticks atomic seconds but inserts leap seconds to stay within 0.9 s of UT1.




Lifted from the LASP Time presentation (Bershenyi/Moffatt, 2026), slides 9-12. The key point: UTC is a compromise — atomic tick rate, solar alignment — and the compromise is paid for with discontinuities.

title: Session 2: Time
section: The cost of the compromise: leap seconds
text:
The cost of the compromise: leap seconds










A leap-second day has 86 401 seconds. In 2022 the CGPM decided to let UT1 − UTC grow beyond 1 s by 2035, effectively ending leap seconds; the LSK still matters for every date before then.


The data in this plot are the DELTET/DELTA_AT table in the LSK. Ask: what does your code do with 23:59:60? Python’s datetime cannot represent it. SPICE can: str2et accepts it.

title: Session 2: Time
section: Time for physics: TT, TDB and ET
text:
Time for physics: TT, TDB and ET






flowchart LR
  UTC["UTC<br/>civil time"] -->|"+ leap seconds<br/>(LSK table)"| TAI["TAI<br/>atomic"]
  TAI -->|"+ 32.184 s<br/>(fixed)"| TT["TT / TDT<br/>Earth-surface<br/>proper time"]
  TT -->|"+ periodic term<br/>≤ 1.7 ms"| TDB["TDB = ET<br/>solar-system<br/>barycentric"]







Equations of motion need a uniform time at the solar-system barycenter: TDB.
ET in SPICE = TDB seconds past J2000 (2000-01-01 12:00:00 TDB).
UTC is only an input/output format; SPICE computes in ET.
Everything on this slide is in the LSK — four numbers plus the leap-second table.


TDB differs from TT because clocks on Earth tick at different rates as Earth moves in the Sun’s gravity well over its eccentric orbit (general relativity). The amplitude is about 1.66 ms with an annual period. DELTET/K, EB and M in the LSK are the coefficients of that periodic term.

title: Session 2: Time
text:
In SpiceyPy

et = sp.str2et("2016-12-31T23:59:60")          # UTC string -> ET (TDB s past J2000)
print(f"ET            = {et:,.3f} s")
print(f"ET - UTC      = {sp.deltet(et, 'ET'):.6f} s")
print(f"one second on = {sp.et2utc(et + 1, 'ISOC', 3)}")
print(f"as DOY        = {sp.timout(et, 'YYYY-DOY // HR:MN:SC.### ::UTC')}")

ET            = 536,500,868.184 s
ET - UTC      = 68.183930 s
one second on = 2017-01-01T00:00:00.000
as DOY        = 2016-366 // 23:59:60.000



Rule of thumb: convert to ET at the edge of your program, do all arithmetic in ET, convert back to UTC only for display.


Point out that adding 1 second to the leap second rolls over to the new year correctly. Doing the same with UTC strings or Unix time would silently be off by one.

title: Session 2: Time
text:
How a spacecraft keeps time






flowchart LR
  OSC["Crystal oscillator<br/>(oven-controlled)"] --> CNT["Counter<br/>seconds : subticks"]
  CNT --> FSW["Flight software<br/>distributes time"]
  FSW --> PKT["Every telemetry packet<br/>stamped with SCLK"]
  FSW --> CMD["Stored commands<br/>execute on SCLK"]







No GPS in deep space and no atomic clock on most missions.
The counter just counts oscillator cycles since some epoch or reset.
An on-board “second” is whatever the oscillator says it is.


The SCLK is not a time scale in the physics sense; it is a counter. Everything downstream — packet time tags, CK time tags, command timing — is expressed in it. That is why SCLK kernels are mission-specific and why CKs are indexed by SCLK ticks, not ET (comes back in Session 5).

title: Session 2: Time
text:
Reading a clock string: MAVEN


3/0812345678.32768



Field
Meaning
Modulus




1
whole on-board seconds
4 294 967 296 (2³²)


2
subticks of 1/65 536 s
65 536




.32768 is 32768 / 65536 = 0.5 s, not 0.32768 s
One tick = 1/65 536 s ≈ 15.3 µs


From MVN_SCLKSCET.00133.tsc:
SCLK01_N_FIELDS_202  = ( 2 )
SCLK01_MODULI_202    = ( 4294967296
                         65536 )
SCLK01_OFFSETS_202   = ( 0 0 )
SCLK01_TIME_SYSTEM_202 = ( 2 )
202 is MAVEN’s clock ID (spacecraft −202). Time system 2 = TDT (TT).


The LASP Time deck has the same warning with a 1/256 subtick: “001 may not be 0.001 seconds”. The kernel, not the programmer, knows the moduli — which is why SPICE clock strings (scs2e) are safer than hand decoding.

title: Session 2: Time
text:
Clocks drift

Oscillator frequency shifts with temperature, aging and radiation.
Small fractional errors add up fast:




≈ 2 ppm

MAVEN’s current rate: 1.0000020 TT s per clock second


≈ 0.17 s/day

how far MAVEN’s clock falls behind TT each day




So “SCLK + 86 400” is not one day later. Convert to ET, add, convert back.




Numbers from the last coefficient rows of MAVEN SCLK kernel 00133 (Dec 2025): rates around 1.0000019 to 1.0000021. 2.07e-6 × 86400 s ≈ 0.18 s/day. MAVEN never slews its clock; the ground model absorbs the drift.

title: Session 2: Time
text:
Correlation: measuring the drift






sequenceDiagram
  participant SC as MAVEN
  participant DSN as DSN station
  participant Ops as Ground ops
  SC->>DSN: frame stamped SCLK = s
  Note over SC,DSN: one-way light time 4–22 min
  DSN->>Ops: received at UTC r
  Ops->>Ops: sent at r − OWLT − station/transponder delays
  Ops->>Ops: record pair (s, TT)






Thousands of these pairs over weeks give a drift history.

OWLT comes from the spacecraft and Earth ephemerides — so time correlation already depends on SPK data (Session 3). The station and on-board delays are calibrated constants. LASP’s MAVEN ops produce the SCLKvSCET file that NAIF’s MAKCLK turns into the kernel.

title: Session 2: Time
text:
The model: piecewise-linear segments










Simulated clock: 2 ppm mean drift (≈ 41 s over 240 days, removed in the top panel) plus a 90-day thermal cycle. A new segment starts whenever a straight line can no longer stay within tolerance.


This is exactly the picture in the LASP deck (slides 27-33), but computed. The orange polyline is what goes in the SCLK kernel. Notebook 02 has participants read the real MAVEN table; Session 7 builds one from this kind of simulation.

title: Session 2: Time
section: That table is the SCLK kernel
text:
That table is the SCLK kernel
Last rows of SCLK01_COEFFICIENTS_202 in MVN_SCLKSCET.00133.tsc (147 rows in total):
    SCLK (ticks)          TT (s past J2000)       rate (TT s / clock s)
5.2781429716173E+13     8.0538118401500E+08     1.0000020628093E+00
5.2854406018253E+13     8.0649471631200E+08     1.0000020810872E+00
5.3088007976141E+13     8.1005920673000E+08     1.0000020691935E+00
5.3296981439693E+13     8.1324789532800E+08     1.0000019830000E+00
Each row starts a segment. For a tick count s inside it:

TT(s) = TT0 + rate × (s − s0) / 65 536

scs2e finds the segment, applies the line, and converts TT → TDB (ET).

Rate units are parallel-time seconds per most-significant clock count (one on-board second for MAVEN), per the SCLK Required Reading. Ticks count the finest field, hence the divide by 65536. The last row is the extrapolation used for times after the latest correlation — which is why reprocessing with a newer SCLK can move recent timestamps.

title: Session 2: Time
text:
Partitions: when the clock resets

A reset, rollover or “jam” breaks the count → start a new partition.
Clock strings carry the partition: 3/0812345678.32768.
MAVEN has 3 partitions (pre-launch and early cruise; 2013-12 to early 2022; current).

SCLK_PARTITION_START_202 = ( 0.0000000000000E+00
                             2.8794165854208E+13
                             4.5804921290752E+13 )

Without a partition number, scs2e assumes the first partition that contains the count; ambiguous counts are a classic bug after a reset. The LASP deck notes Kepler added two partitions in a single year after safe-mode resets.

title: Session 2: Time
section: Three ways LASP missions handle drift
text:
Three ways LASP missions handle drift








Strategy
Example missions
Trade-off




Discipline the clock to GPS
MMS, IXPE
Easiest; GPS only near Earth


Adjust the on-board clock
SORCE (formerly AIM)
Small time jumps on board; ground model stays simple


Leave the clock alone; model it on the ground
MAVEN, EMM, Kepler
Clean on-board time; ground needs an up-to-date SCLK




From the LASP Time presentation (Bershenyi/Moffatt, 2026).


Ask the room which category their mission is in. For GPS-disciplined missions the “SCLK kernel” may be trivial (MMS VTC = TAI), but the concept still applies.

title: Session 2: Time
text:
Why it matters



7.5 m

along-track error per 1 ms of timing error in LEO (7.5 km/s)


~700 m

MAVEN near periapsis (~4 km/s) if one day of drift (0.17 s) were ignored


Pointing error scales with slew rate the same way.
CK attitude is indexed by SCLK: a stale SCLK mis-times and mis-points.

title: Session 2: Time
text:
In SpiceyPy (notebook 02)
sp.furnsh(["naif0012.tls", "MVN_SCLKSCET.00133.tsc"])

et  = sp.scs2e(-202, "3/0812345678.32768")   # clock string -> ET
utc = sp.et2utc(et, "ISOC", 3)
clk = sp.sce2s(-202, et)                     # ET -> clock string

coeffs = sp.gdpool("SCLK01_COEFFICIENTS_202", 0, 1000).reshape(-1, 3)

Spacecraft ID −202 selects MAVEN’s clock (clock ID 202). Always load the newest SCLK for reprocessing.

text:

title: Course Plan
text: Seven sessions take developers from “what is a kernel” to computing instrument geometry with kernels produced by other teams, plus an advanced final session on building their own SCLK, SPK and CK files. All work is in Python with SpiceyPy. Each session pairs NAIF self-training readings with a background primer on the physics or math NAIF assumes you already know, and a runnable notebook.

title: Course Plan
text:
Overview

Audience: LASP developers comfortable in Python; little or no prior SPICE internals knowledge.
Format: book club. Participants read before each session; the session itself is ~60 minutes: 10 min Q&A on the previous notebook, 20 min background talk, 25 min discussion of the reading, 5 min preview. Notebooks are homework, done in the week after each session alongside the next reading.
Cadence: every two weeks; seven sessions total (six core, one advanced and optional).
The gap this fills: NAIF’s tutorials explain how to use SPICE but rarely why the data look the way they do. Each session adds a primer on that missing context: how spacecraft keep time, why light-time matters, the linear algebra behind frames, and how attitude is measured on board.
Running example: MAVEN, a LASP-operated mission with public kernels (SCLK, SPK, CK, FK, IK) on the NAIF server. Using one real spacecraft throughout ties the abstractions to data people recognize.
Existing LASP material reused: an internal 2026 LASP Time presentation (Bershenyi/Moffatt) covering time history, UTC vs. TAI, spacecraft clock drift and the piecewise-linear SCLK model. It anchors Session 2.

title: Course Plan
text:
Session 1: SPICE architecture and kernels
Goal: everyone leaves with a working environment, a meta-kernel, and a mental model of SPICE as “a database of geometry, queried by time.”
Reading: tutorials 03 (overview), 05 slides 4 and 7–9 (text vs. binary kernels, common synonyms, kernel file names and extensions; keep slide 7 handy as a glossary), 06 (NAIF IDs), 08 (intro to the toolkit), 12 (kernels), 13 (comments), 14 (API headers). Skim 01, 07 and 11 for setup only; 36 (WebGeocalc) optional. Slides: Session 1: Architecture and kernels.
Background primer: what problem is SPICE solving?

Every science measurement needs ancillary answers: where was the spacecraft, where was it pointing, what time was it, what was in the field of view, was the target lit. These come from different teams (navigation, attitude, instrument, timing) at different cadences.
SPICE’s design answer: each kind of ancillary data lives in its own kernel type, produced by whoever owns it, and the toolkit combines them at query time. That is why one question can need 6–10 files.
Developer framing: kernels are a read-only, file-backed key-value store keyed by (object ID, frame, time). The kernel pool is global state, which explains why load order, furnsh/kclear, and thread safety matter.
Text vs. binary kernels, and why both exist (human-editable constants vs. large, fast-to-search arrays).

Discussion prompts

Which kernel types does your current project touch, even indirectly (e.g. through time_convert)?
Why does SPICE use integer NAIF IDs rather than names internally? What breaks if two kernels disagree on a name–ID mapping?
What are the risks of SPICE’s global kernel pool in a long-running service or a multi-threaded pipeline?

Notebook 01_kernels_and_ids

Install check: spiceypy.tkvrsn('TOOLKIT').
Download generic kernels (LSK, de440s.bsp, pck00011.tpc) with a small cached helper.
Write a meta-kernel by hand, load it, and list what is loaded with ktotal / kdata.
Name–ID lookups: bodn2c, bodc2n; spacecraft vs. body vs. instrument ID ranges.
First geometry query: Earth–Moon distance over a month, plotted.
Read kernel comments programmatically; inspect a binary SPK with spkobj / spkcov.
Exercise: load the MAVEN FK and find every instrument ID it defines.

title: Course Plan
text:
Session 2: Time
Goal: participants can explain why an SCLK kernel exists before they ever open one, and can read a real SCLK kernel as a history of the spacecraft’s clock.
Reading: tutorial 04 slides 4–13 (time concepts: TAI, UTC, UT1, leap seconds, TDB, TDT, spacecraft clocks), then 15 (time) and 16 (LSK and SCLK); SPICE Time Subsystem and SCLK Required Reading (sections on clock strings, partitions and coefficients). Slides: Session 2: Time.
Background primer: how time works, on the ground and on a spacecraft

Two ways to count time. Solar time (UT1) follows Earth’s irregular rotation; atomic time (TAI) counts uniform SI seconds. UTC is TAI with leap seconds inserted to stay within 0.9 s of UT1; TAI − UTC = 37 s since 2017.
Time for dynamics. Equations of motion need a uniform time. TT = TAI + 32.184 s; TDB differs from TT by a periodic relativistic term of about 1.7 ms. SPICE’s ET is TDB seconds past J2000 (2000-01-01 12:00:00 TDB). Why UTC is a format, not a computational time scale, in SPICE.
How a spacecraft keeps time. A crystal oscillator drives a counter; the counter is split into fields (e.g. seconds + 1/65536 subticks) stamped into every telemetry packet. Oscillators drift with temperature and age, so a “second” on board is not an SI second.
Correlation. The ground records when a packet arrives; subtract one-way light time and station delays to get when it left, and pair that with the on-board count. Many such pairs give a drift history.
The model. Fit piecewise-linear segments (SCLK value, parallel time, rate). A clock reset starts a new partition. This is exactly the SCLK kernel’s coefficient table.
The three operational strategies: GPS-disciplined clock (MMS), adjust the on-board clock (SORCE), or leave the clock alone and model it on the ground (MAVEN, EMM, Kepler).
Why it matters: at 7.5 km/s in LEO, a 1 ms timing error is 7.5 m of along-track error; for pointing, it scales with slew rate.

Discussion prompts

Why does SPICE refuse to let you add 86400 to an SCLK and call it “one day later”?
What changes for MAVEN, whose clock is never slewed, versus a smallsat whose time is reset from the ground?
What would happen to your software if leap seconds were abolished (CGPM 2022 decision, by 2035)?

Notebook 02_time_and_sclk

str2et, et2utc, timout picture strings; deltet to show ET − UTC.
Plot TAI − UTC from the LSK across 1972–today; show a time across a leap second (23:59:60).
Load the MAVEN SCLK; convert clock strings with scs2e / sce2s; decode the fields and moduli from the kernel.
Read the drift history: pull MAVEN’s coefficient table with gdpool (SCLK01_COEFFICIENTS_202), plot the clock rate per segment across the mission, and mark partition boundaries.
Convert the same packet time with two SCLK versions to see why reprocessing needs the latest SCLK.
Exercise: how large is the position error for MAVEN at periapsis if the SCLK is off by 20 ms?

title: Course Plan
text:
Session 3: Ephemerides (SPK)
Goal: participants understand an SPK as interpolated trajectory data with a center-of-motion chain, can check what a delivered SPK actually covers, and know when aberration corrections matter.
Reading: tutorial 04 slides 25 (state vectors) and 28–40 (aberration corrections; skim the effect tables on 37–40), then 18 (SPK); Aberration Corrections Required Reading (intro and examples only). 42 (making an SPK) moves to Session 7.
Background primer: positions as data

State vectors. Position + velocity relative to a center, in a frame, at a time. Every SPK query has all four parts; most bugs come from getting one implicitly wrong.
Where trajectories come from. Navigation teams fit orbits to radiometric tracking (range, Doppler, delta-DOR) and propagate forward; planetary ephemerides (DE440) are fits to decades of observations.
Storing a trajectory. Segments of Chebyshev polynomials (planets), Hermite or Lagrange interpolation of discrete states (spacecraft), or two-line elements (Earth orbiters). Accuracy vs. file size trade-offs.
The center chain. MAVEN relative to Mars barycenter, relative to the solar-system barycenter. SPICE walks the tree and adds vectors; a missing link is the classic “insufficient ephemeris data” error.
Segment priority. Later-loaded segments win, which is how predicts and reconstructions coexist.
Light-time and stellar aberration. Light from Mars is 3–22 minutes old. LT+S gives the apparent direction an instrument sees; NONE gives the geometric truth. Show the size: tens of arcseconds for stellar aberration, thousands of km of light-time displacement for planets.

Discussion prompts

When should a science pipeline use NONE vs. LT+S? Who decides for your mission?
How would you detect that a predict SPK is still loaded over a reconstruction?

Notebook 03_spk_ephemeris

spkezr / spkpos for planets; plot inner-solar-system orbits.
Inspect coverage and segments of a MAVEN SPK (spkcov, brief-style summary).
Plot MAVEN’s orbit around Mars over a day; find periapsis altitude.
Compare NONE, LT, LT+S for Mars from Earth and quantify the differences.
Audit a delivery: find coverage gaps in a set of MAVEN SPKs and tell predicts from reconstructions using their comments.
Exercise: load a predict and a reconstruction in both orders and show how segment priority changes the answer.

title: Course Plan
text:
Session 4: Rotations and reference frames
Goal: participants can move fluently between rotation matrices, Euler angles, axis-angle and quaternions, and know which convention SPICE uses for each.
Reading: tutorial 04 slides 14–21 (reference frames: centers, types, J2000/ICRF, body-fixed, topocentric) and 26–27 (transforming states); tutorial 05 slides 12–13 (right-handed frames, quaternion styles); then 17 (frames and coordinate systems) and 21 (FK); the written rotation primer. Optional: 19 (PCK), Rotation and Frames Required Reading, 24 (dynamic frames), NAIF’s quaternion white paper.
Background primer: the math of orientation
In the 20-minute talk (four ideas):

Frames as bases. A frame is an origin plus three orthonormal axes. A rotation matrix is orthogonal: its inverse is its transpose, det R = +1.
Passive vs. active. SPICE’s pxform re-expresses a fixed vector in a new frame (passive); many libraries rotate the vector (active). Same matrix, opposite sign of angle: the most common source of bugs.
Composition and the frame tree. R(A→C) = R(B→C) · R(A→B); SPICE chains inertial, body-fixed, spacecraft and instrument frames this way.
Quaternions and their conventions. Four numbers, no singularities, cheap to compose; why telemetry and CKs use them. SPICE is scalar-first Hamilton; most attitude telemetry is scalar-last with the opposite rotation sense.

In the written primer (read before the session, not presented): Euler angles and gimbal lock; axis-angle and Rodrigues’ formula; SLERP and the q/−q double cover; SPICE’s own active vs. passive routines (rotate/rotvec vs. axisar/vrotv); rotating states and the ω × r term behind sxform.
Discussion prompts

Find a quaternion in your own telemetry. Is it scalar-first or scalar-last? Active or passive? How do you know?
Why does IAU_MARS need a PCK but J2000 does not?

Notebook 04_rotations_and_frames

Interactive 3D widget: drag Euler angles, watch the axes, matrix and quaternion update together.
Round-trip conversions (eul2m/m2eul, m2q/q2m) and a numeric check of orthogonality.
Convert an engineering quaternion to SPICE form and verify against a known pointing.
pxform('J2000', 'IAU_MARS', et): inspect the frame chain behind it.
Exercise: compute a ground station’s position in J2000 from its latitude and longitude.

Moved out: gimbal lock and SLERP demos become optional extras; writing a TK frame moves to Session 7.

title: Course Plan
section: Session 5: Attitude and instruments (CK, FK, IK)
text:
Session 5: Attitude and instruments (CK, FK, IK)
Goal: participants can trace a pixel on an instrument back through the instrument, spacecraft and inertial frames, and can diagnose why a pointing query fails or looks wrong.
Reading: tutorials 20 (CK), 22 (using frames), 25 (IK), 26 (reading FKs and IKs). Revisit 21 (FK) for CK-based and fixed-offset frames, and tutorial 04 slides 15–16 (frame centers and frame types). Tutorial 05 slide 15 covers quoting strings in text kernels, which you’ll see in every FK and IK. 43 (making a CK) moves to Session 7.
Background primer: how a spacecraft knows where it points

Sensors. Star trackers give absolute attitude (arcseconds) at a few Hz; gyros give rates at high cadence but drift; sun sensors and magnetometers give coarse vectors. On-board estimators (usually a Kalman filter) fuse them and output a quaternion in telemetry.
Control. Reaction wheels and thrusters execute slews; the commanded profile (predict CK) differs from what happened (reconstructed CK).
Rigid-body transforms. A pose is rotation plus translation; robotics packs it into a 4×4 homogeneous matrix. SPICE splits it: translations live in SPKs (or are ignored for instrument offsets), rotations in CKs and FKs. Discuss when the instrument’s physical offset from the spacecraft center matters (rarely for remote sensing, sometimes for close flybys or in-situ instruments).
The structure chain. Inertial → spacecraft bus (CK) → articulating platform (CK) → instrument mount (fixed FK) → detector (IK geometry). Alignment calibrations update the fixed links.
Time again. CK time tags are SCLK ticks, so Session 2 comes back: a wrong SCLK kernel silently mis-points every observation.
CK practicalities. Discrete vs. continuous types, interpolation intervals, gaps, and the tolerance argument in ckgp.

Discussion prompts

Where in your mission’s data flow does a telemetry quaternion become a CK? Who validates it?
How would you tell whether a pointing error comes from the CK, the FK alignment, or the SCLK?

Notebook 05_ck_fk_ik

Load MAVEN CK, FK, IK and SCLK; get spacecraft attitude with pxform and coverage with ckcov.
Read an IK with getfov; draw the instrument boresight and field of view on a Mars globe.
Follow the frame chain explicitly with frinfo and pxform at each link.
Diagnose pointing: find CK coverage gaps, see how the ckgp tolerance and interpolation intervals change results, and decode “no pointing available” errors.
Introduce a deliberate 50 ms SCLK error and measure the resulting pointing error.
Exercise: list which MAVEN frames are fixed offsets vs. CK-based, and which kernel supplies each link.

title: Course Plan
section: Session 6: Derived geometry and event finding
text:
Session 6: Derived geometry and event finding
Goal: participants combine every kernel type to answer real observation-planning questions, and know how to debug when SPICE says no.
Reading: tutorial 04 slides 22–24 (planetocentric, planetodetic and planetographic coordinates), then 27 (derived quantities), 29 (Geometry Finder), 30 (toolkit apps), 32 (exceptions), 33 (common problems), 37 (DSK). Skim 35 (summary of key points).
Background primer: from vectors to answers

Shape models. Triaxial ellipsoids (PCK radii) vs. plate models (DSK); where each is good enough.
Surface geometry. Sub-observer and sub-solar points, ray–surface intercepts, and the incidence, emission and phase angles every remote-sensing scientist asks for.
Searching over time. GF treats geometry as a function of time and finds when a condition holds: root-finding with a step size you must choose. Too large a step misses short events.
Errors as information. SPICE’s error subsystem, SpiceyError in Python, and reading a traceback to find the missing kernel.
Toolkit utilities as debugging tools: brief, ckbrief, chronos, spacit, spkdiff.

Discussion prompts

What questions does your team currently answer with ad-hoc code that GF could answer directly?
What makes a GF step size safe for MAVEN’s ~4.5-hour orbit?

Notebook 06_geometry_finder

Sub-spacecraft ground track of MAVEN over Mars with subpnt; color by local solar time.
Illumination angles at the boresight intercept with sincpt and ilumin.
Find periapsis passes (gfdist) and Mars occultations as seen from a DSN station (gfoclt).
Swap the ellipsoid for a DSK and compare intercept altitudes.
Trigger and decode three common errors (missing LSK, no SPK coverage, wrong frame name).

Capstone (optional take-home): each pair picks a question from their own work, writes a small notebook answering it, and presents it in 5 minutes at a follow-up session.

title: Course Plan
text:
Session 7 (advanced, optional): Making kernels
Goal: participants who produce or validate kernels understand how SCLK, SPK, CK and FK files are built, and can review a delivered kernel critically. Pure kernel users can skip it.
Reading: tutorials 42 (making an SPK) and 43 (making a CK); the mkspk and msopck parts of 30; SCLK Required Reading (coefficients and partitions); revisit 13 (comments).
Background primer: where kernels come from

Production pipelines. Tracking data → navigation solution → SPK; attitude telemetry → CK; time correlation → SCLK; alignment calibration → FK. Who owns each step for LASP missions vs. JPL navigation or the spacecraft vendor.
Design choices. SPK and CK types, interpolation degree, segment boundaries, and file size vs. accuracy.
Quaternion conventions when writing CKs, revisiting Session 4.
Validation and provenance. Comments as metadata, version and naming conventions, and checks such as spkdiff, frmdiff and ckbrief before a kernel enters a pipeline.

Discussion prompt: what checks would you require before accepting a delivered kernel into your data system?
Notebook 07_making_kernels

SCLK: simulate an oscillator with thermal drift and noisy correlation points, fit piecewise-linear segments within 50 ms, write a text SCLK, and compare scs2e against truth; add a clock reset to create a new partition.
SPK: propagate a Keplerian orbit and write it with spkw09; write an Earth orbiter from a TLE with spkw10; compare with an mkspk setup file.
CK: convert simulated engineering-style quaternion telemetry to SPICE quaternions, write with ckw03, and verify the boresight sweep.
FK: define a fixed-offset instrument frame and check where it points.
Add provenance comments and run validation checks on each file.

title: Session 1: Architecture and kernels
text:
One row of science data
An IUVS spectrum from MAVEN, time-tagged by the spacecraft clock.
To turn it into science, someone has to answer:



When was it taken, in UTC?
Where was MAVEN?
Which way was it pointing?



What did the slit see: limb, disk, sky?
What was the solar zenith angle there?
How far was the light from the target?






None of these answers is in the science packet. They are ancillary data, and each one comes from a different team.




Start from a measurement everyone in the data systems group has handled. The point: the science file is only useful once it is joined with geometry, and that geometry is somebody else’s product.

Different owners, different update rates, different sizes, different formats. SPICE’s whole design follows from this table.


Ask the room who on the team has touched each of these, even indirectly. Most will say “time_convert” or “some geometry library” without knowing which kernels sat behind it.

title: Session 1: Architecture and kernels
text:
SPICE’s design answer






flowchart LR
  NAV[Navigation] --> SPK[(SPK)]
  OPS[Spacecraft ops] --> CK[(CK)]
  TC[Time correlation] --> SCLK[(SCLK)]
  INST[Instrument team] --> IK[(FK / IK)]
  IERS[IERS / IAU] --> LSK[(LSK / PCK)]
  SPK & CK & SCLK & IK & LSK --> POOL{{"kernel pool<br/>(in your process)"}}
  POOL --> API["spkpos, sincpt,<br/>scs2e, ..."]
  API --> YOU[Your code]







Each kind of ancillary data lives in its own file type, produced and versioned by whoever owns it. The toolkit combines them only at query time.

title: Session 1: Architecture and kernels
text:
Why one answer needs 6–10 files
“Where did the IUVS boresight hit Mars at this clock tick, and was it lit?”



Step
Kernel




clock tick → ET
SCLK + LSK


MAVEN relative to Mars
SPK (MAVEN) + SPK (planets)


spacecraft attitude
CK (indexed by SCLK)


boresight in spacecraft frame
FK + IK


Mars shape and orientation
PCK (or DSK)




Miss any one and the call fails, loudly. That is a feature: SPICE errors name the missing piece.

title: Session 1: Architecture and kernels
text:
A developer’s model



Kernels are a read-only, file-backed store keyed by (object ID, reference frame, time). Each API call is a query against everything loaded.



import spiceypy as sp

sp.furnsh("session01.tm")                          # load a list of kernels

et = sp.str2et("2026-11-19T12:00:00")               # query 1: time   (LSK)
pos, lt = sp.spkpos("MOON", et, "J2000",            # query 2: state  (SPK)
                    "NONE", "EARTH")
No file names appear in the queries. The kernel pool decides which file answers.

title: Session 1: Architecture and kernels
section: The kernel pool is global state
text:
The kernel pool is global state


What that means

One pool per process; every function sees it.
kclear() empties it for everyone.
Data loaded later win when two kernels cover the same thing.


Why developers care

Load once, at startup, in one place.
CSPICE is not thread-safe: one SPICE caller per process, or a lock.
Log what you loaded (ktotal / kdata); it is your provenance.



This is the slide most relevant to the data systems group. Long-running services, Dask workers and multiprocessing pools all trip over the global pool. Keep the deeper discussion for the discussion block.

title: Session 1: Architecture and kernels
text:
Two kinds of files









Text kernels
Binary kernels




Types
LSK, SCLK, PCK (text), FK, IK, meta-kernel
SPK, CK, PCK (binary), DSK


Format
KEY = value assignments in \begindata blocks
DAF/DAS arrays with a comment area


Size
kilobytes
megabytes to gigabytes


Edited by
people, in an editor
programs (mkspk, msopck, spkw*)


Why
constants humans review and diff
dense time series searched fast




Text kernels can be read and diffed like code. Binary kernels can’t: inspect them with toolkit utilities (brief, ckbrief, commnt) or API calls, never a text editor.

Patterns: barycenters 1–9 · Sun 10 · planets P99 · moons P01–98 · spacecraft negative · instruments −SSSxxx · ground stations 399xxx. Mission kernels add names (e.g. MAVEN_IUVS).


The table is computed live with bodn2c: these mappings are built into the toolkit. Ask: why both 4 and 499 for Mars? Answer next session in SPK land: the planetary SPK gives barycenters; the planet-to-barycenter offset is a separate file.

title: Session 1: Architecture and kernels
section: Meta-kernels: the list is the provenance
text:
Meta-kernels: the list is the provenance
KPL/MK
\begindata
   PATH_VALUES     = ( '../kernels' )
   PATH_SYMBOLS    = ( 'KERNELS' )
   KERNELS_TO_LOAD = ( '$KERNELS/naif0012.tls'
                       '$KERNELS/pck00011.tpc'
                       '$KERNELS/de440s.bsp' )
\begintext

One furnsh loads them all, in this order: later files have priority.
Relative paths resolve against the working directory, not the .tm file.
Version the meta-kernel with your code; it records exactly which data you used.

title: Session 1: Architecture and kernels
text:
Read before you trust


Comments
Who made the file, from what, valid when, known problems.

text kernels: outside \begindata
binary kernels: comment area (commnt, dafec)


Coverage
What the file actually contains.

spkobj / spkcov for SPK
ckobj / ckcov for CK
brief, ckbrief on the command line





Most “SPICE is broken” reports are a kernel that doesn’t cover the time asked for, or the wrong version loaded. Check both first.
